Spec Kit is GitHub's free, open source toolkit (MIT, 147K stars) for what they call spec driven development, and it works with Claude Code plus dozens of other coding agents. Instead of one big prompt and a hopeful build, you work in five commands, in order: constitution sets your rules (quality, testing, what not to touch), specify turns your plain English idea into a written spec, plan picks the stack and approach, tasks breaks it into a checklist, and implement builds from that checklist. It also has a bug flow and an "is this idea worth building" assessment that ends in go, clarify or stop. The habit that matters: read the spec and the task list before you let it build. Fixing a sentence takes ten seconds, fixing a wrong feature takes an afternoon. What's the last thing AI built for you that wasn't what you asked for? #github #aitools #ai #agilesingh

Keep pauses that serve the meaning. Don't speed up my voice. 3. Word-by-word subtitles in my style. 4. If references/music.mp3 exists, put it quietly under the voice. 5. Graphics only where they help. 6. Export 1080x1920 to done as draft-v1.mp4 plus edit-notes.md. Check the file, then show me. Save my fixes as draft-v2, draft-v3. How Cloudflare's Code Mode Supercharges MCP! 🤖⚡ Despite claims that Cloudflare's Code Mode replaces the Model Context Protocol (MCP), it actually makes MCP dramatically more efficient. In a traditional setup, an AI agent loads thousands of tokens of tool descriptions upfront and executes actions one round trip at a time. Asking a model to schedule 31 distinct calendar events forces 31 separate inference loops, re-sending the entire conversation history and tool schemas on every single step. Code Mode eliminates this bottleneck by automatically converting MCP tool definitions into standard programming functions, allowing the model to write one short script with a loop instead of making dozens of individual tool calls. That generated script runs inside an isolated sandbox with no open internet access, communicating exclusively with the underlying MCP server under the agent's existing permissions. The program handles all 31 API calls locally and returns a brief summary to the model, slashing token usage by 81 percent. This pattern also solves massive context bloat at enterprise scale. Rather than stuffing over a million tokens of schemas for 2,500 platform actions into a prompt, Cloudflare's own MCP server exposes just two tools, one to search for actions and one to execute code, shrinking the footprint to roughly a thousand tokens. #ModelContextProtocol #Cloudflare #AIAgents #SoftwareEngineering #SystemDesign #TechExplained

transcript_with_timestamp.text: Two weeks ago, a free repository called REA,
short for Reverse Engineer anything,
quietly went nuclear on Github,
exploding past 115,000 stars and 25,000 forks in a matter of days.
With a single terminal command,
it connects AI coding agents
directly into the US National Security Agency's binary decompiler,
allowing anyone to take a locked
closed source dot exe app or video game
and strip mine it back into clean
C++ source code in less than 48 hours.
Developers are already using it to mass decompile commercial games
and crack proprietary hardware.
But when independent researchers ran 482 controlled tests on this tool
just days ago, they uncovered a twist
that proves closed source software isn't just vulnerable,
it might already be dead.
Up until this month,
if you wanted to use AI to clone a piece of paid software,
you had to vibe code it.
You showed an AI a screenshot of Photoshop or a video game,
and the AI tried to guess how the code worked from the outside.
For simple apps, that worked.
But the moment an application had complex game physics,
custom audio engines, or encrypted network checks,
the AI hit a brick wall because it couldn't see the actual source code
locked inside the dot exe file.
Normally, when a studio finishes writing a program,
they run it through a compiler that strips away every folder,
every variable name, and every human word,
crushing the code down into millions of lines of raw machine assembly.
Even if you dropped that file into elite forensic tools like IDA Pro
or the NSA's GDB Decompiler,
all you got back was a scrambled maze of anonymous memory addresses
that took human hackers years to decipher by hand.
REA bypassed that human bottleneck overnight.
Built by a developer named Morluto,
the tool uses the Model Context Protocol,
or MCP to give AI agents like Claude Code open
AI Codex and cursor direct handson control over Guider,
IDA Pro, Binwalk,
and live network interceptors.
Instead of a human staring at nameless assembly code for six months,
the AI agent opens the binary inside guider,
headlessly
traces thousands of function calls across the memory graph in seconds,
and rewrites the unreadable assembly back into clean C++ or rust.
Even crazier, it doesn't guess.
In a test on the classic PC game DX Ball,
the agent extracted a compiled X 86 audio routine,
rebuild it in Clean Sea, tested it against 3,205 execution states,
and matched 63 out of 63 original compiled bytes with 100% accuracy.
And within hours of that demo going live,
the gaming underground turned it loose on commercial games.
Wait until you see what happened
when game modders got their hands on this workflow.
Historically,
decompiling a single video game back into native source code
was one of the hardest feats in computer science.
When fans manually decompiled Super Mario 64 and Zelda Ocarina of time,
it took teams of programmers years of agonizing work.
Therefore, only a Handful of legendary games were ever decompiled.
Two weeks ago, that multi year barrier collapsed into a single weekend.
Look at a viral project called Isaac Recomp.
The original
2011 version of the binding of Isaac was built inside dead
Adobe Flash code,
permanently trapped at a laggy 30 frames per second and a blurry
low resolution. A developer pointed an A I
decompilation pipeline straight at the game's binary
and automatically translated the entire code base into native C++
in just days, right out of the box.
A 15 year old flash game was running natively on modern PCs
at 1440 p and a locked 165 frames per second,
and Isaac Recomp was just the opening shot.
Within days,
Hacker News and Github were flooded with AI decompiled game engines.
One developer used AI
and gedit to reconstruct the proprietary Refractor 2 engine
from Battlefield 2 into modern C++.
Twenty another extracted a full 3D engine from Subway Surfers,
another translated the cult classic shooter
Gun Zed the duel straight into memory safe rust,
while a new experimental project called any PS five
launched with a wild goal
using automated binary translation
to convert PlayStation console executables.
